subject: English Language
topic: Sample Narrative Essay: A Day to Remember
content: The morning sun began its ascent, casting long, golden shadows across the dusty streets of Mbare. It was a day I would never forget. My heart was thumping against my ribs like a trapped bird as I clutched my results slip. I had spent years studying by the flickering light of a candle, and today was the moment of truth. As I approached the school gates, the familiar scent of woodsmoke and roasting maize filled the air, usually a comfort, but today it felt suffocating. I found my name on the list pinned to the notice board. My eyes blurred for a second. There it was: 'A' in English, 'A' in Mathematics, 'A' in Science. A wave of pure, unadulterated joy washed over me, drowning out the noise of the bustling market nearby. I sprinted all the way home, my feet barely touching the ground. When I reached our small house, my mother was hanging laundry. One look at my face and she knew. We didn't need words; we just held each other, the tears of struggle finally turning into tears of triumph. That day taught me that while our circumstances may be difficult, our determination defines our destination. It wasn't just about the grades; it was about the door that had finally swung open for my family.

subject: Principles of Accounts
content: In ZIMSEC Accounting, correcting errors is a high-mark topic. Errors that do not affect the Trial Balance (TB) are corrected using a Journal Entry and then posted to the Ledger. 1. Identify the mistake: Was it an Error of Principle (e.g., Motor Vehicle debited to Repairs)? 2. Work out the correct entry: Motor Vehicle should have been debited. 3. Work out how to fix it: Credit Repairs (to remove the wrong entry) and Debit Motor Vehicle (to record the right one). Journal Entry: DR Motor Vehicle, CR Repairs. 4. Narrations: Always add a short description, e.g., 'Being correction of error of principle'. Errors that DO affect the TB (e.g., a one-sided entry or a math error) require a 'Suspense Account'. If the DR side of the TB is $100 less than the CR, you create a Suspense Account with a $100 DR balance. When the error is found (e.g., Sales was under-cast by $100), you fix it by: DR Suspense $100, CR Sales $100. The Suspense Account should eventually have a zero balance once all errors are corrected.

subject: Economics
topic: Inflation in Zimbabwe: Causes and Consequences
content: Inflation is a persistent increase in the general price level. In Zimbabwe, we have experienced both 'Cost-Push' and 'Demand-Pull' inflation. 1. Demand-Pull: Occurs when 'too much money chases too few goods'. This often happens if the money supply grows faster than the real output of the economy. 2. Cost-Push: Occurs when the costs of production rise, such as fuel price hikes or a weakening exchange rate (making imported raw materials expensive). 3. Hyperinflation: An extreme form where prices rise by more than 50% per month, as seen in Zimbabwe in 2008. Consequences: - Loss of purchasing power (money buys less). - Discouragement of savings (money loses value in the bank). - Uncertainty for businesses, which reduces investment. - Fixed-income earners (pensioners/teachers) suffer most. The government and the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) use 'Monetary Policy' (interest rates/money supply control) and 'Fiscal Policy' (budget management) to bring stability. The introduction of the ZiG (Zimbabwe Gold) currency is the latest attempt to curb inflation by backing the currency with physical gold reserves.

subject: Agriculture
topic: Major Cattle Diseases in Zimbabwe and Management
content: Livestock health is essential for a profitable farm. 1. Tick-Borne Diseases: These are the biggest threat. - January Disease (Theileriosis): Symptoms include swelling of lymph nodes, high fever, and death. It is most common in the rainy season. - Redwater: Spread by the blue tick, causes red urine and anemia. - Heartwater: Causes nervous symptoms (circling/convulsions). Management: Strict Dipping (once a week in summer, once a fortnight in winter) using acaricides. 2. Viral Diseases: - Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD): Highly contagious, causes blisters on the mouth and feet. Controlled by vaccination and movement restrictions (quarantine). 3. Bacterial Diseases: - Anthrax: Causes sudden death and bleeding from body openings. Carcasses must be burned or buried deep with lime. DO NOT open the carcass as spores are dangerous to humans. - Blackleg: Causes swelling and lameness. Controlled by annual vaccination of young stock. Farmers must keep a 'Health Record' and report outbreaks to the Veterinary Services department.

subject: Combined Science
content: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes in the external surroundings. Key factors regulated include Body Temperature (37C), Blood Glucose levels, and Water content. 1. Temperature Regulation (Thermoregulation): Controlled by the Hypothalamus in the brain. - When hot: Blood vessels in the skin dilate (Vasodilation) to bring more blood to the surface to lose heat. Sweat glands produce sweat, which cools the skin as it evaporates. Hair lies flat. - When cold: Blood vessels constrict (Vasoconstriction) to keep heat in the core. Shivering (muscle contraction) generates heat. Hair stands up (goosebumps) to trap an insulating layer of air. 2. Blood Glucose: Regulated by the Pancreas. - If glucose is too high, the pancreas releases 'Insulin', which tells the liver to store glucose as Glycogen. - If glucose is too low, it releases 'Glucagon', which converts glycogen back into glucose. This 'Negative Feedback' loop ensures the body stays in balance.

subject: Combined Science
topic: Chemistry: Extraction and Uses of Copper
content: Copper is a vital metal for the electrical industry due to its high conductivity. 1. Extraction: Usually extracted from the ore 'Copper Pyrites' (CuFeS2). The process involves: - Crushing and Grinding the ore. - Froth Flotation: Concentrating the copper-bearing minerals. - Roasting and Smelting: Heating the concentrate to produce 'Blister Copper'. - Refining: Blister copper is about 99% pure but needs 'Electrolytic Refining' to reach 99.99% for electrical use. In electrolysis, the impure copper is the Anode, pure copper is the Cathode, and Copper Sulphate is the electrolyte. 2. Properties: Excellent conductor of heat and electricity, malleable (easy to shape), and resistant to corrosion. 3. Uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and making alloys like Brass (Copper + Zinc) and Bronze (Copper + Tin). Copper is one of the metals Zimbabwe has successfully mined and processed over decades.

subject: Computer Science
topic: Internet Protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and SMTP
content: Protocols are the 'languages' or rules that computers use to talk to each other over the internet. 1. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): The foundation of the World Wide Web. It is used to request and send web pages. 2. HTTPS (Secure): The same as HTTP but encrypted using SSL/TLS. It protects sensitive data like bank passwords and credit card numbers. 3. FTP (File Transfer Protocol): Used specifically for moving files between a client and a server. 4. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol): The standard for sending emails. To receive emails, protocols like POP3 (downloads and deletes from server) or IMAP (syncs with server) are used. 5. IP (Internet Protocol): Responsible for addressing and routing 'packets' of data across the network so they reach the correct destination. Every device on the internet has a unique 'IP Address' (e.g., 192.168.1.1). Understanding these is essential for networking and cybersecurity.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: The First Chimurenga (Umvukela) was a revolutionary war by the Shona and Ndebele people against the British South Africa Company (BSAC) rule. Causes: 1. Loss of Land (the 1894 Land Commission). 2. Cattle Seizures. 3. Forced Labour (Chibharo). 4. Hut Tax. 5. Interference with traditional customs. Key Leaders: The war was guided by spiritual leaders like Mbuya Nehanda and Sekuru Kaguvi (Shona) and Mlimo (Ndebele). Nehanda was based in Mazowe and Kaguvi in the Chishawasha area. The fight was fierce, but the British eventually used superior firepower (Maxim guns) and dynamite to crush the resistance. Nehanda and Kaguvi were captured and executed in 1898. Nehanda's famous dying words, 'My bones shall rise again', became the inspiration for the Second Chimurenga in the 1960s. This war remains a symbol of Zimbabwean resistance and the beginning of the quest for national sovereignty.

subject: Sociology
content: Sociologists disagree on why inequality exists. 1. Functionalism (Talcott Parsons): Stratification is necessary for social order. Different roles have different values, and rewards (pay/status) encourage people to work hard for the most important roles. 2. Davis and Moore: 'Role Allocation'. Society must ensure the most functionally important positions (e.g., Doctors) are filled by the most talented people. 3. Marxism (Karl Marx): Stratification is a tool of oppression. The Bourgeoisie own the 'Means of Production' and exploit the Proletariat. Inequality is not functional; it is harmful and leads to class conflict. 4. Weberianism (Max Weber): Stratification is more than just class. It is 'Multidimensional', involving Class (economic), Status (prestige), and Party (political power). Someone could have high status (e.g., a priest) but low class (income). 5. Tumin's Critique: He argued that it's hard to measure 'functional importance' and that stratification actually prevents talent from rising because the poor lack the opportunity to get educated. These theories are critical for A-Level Sociology essays on inequality.

subject: Commerce
topic: Channels of Distribution and the Middleman
content: Distribution is moving goods from the producer to the final consumer. 1. Traditional Channel: Manufacturer -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer. 2. Direct Channel: Manufacturer -> Consumer (e.g., farm stalls or online shops). 3. Modern Channels: Manufacturer -> Large Retailer (like OK or TM Pick n Pay) -> Consumer. The 'Wholesaler' acts as a middleman who: - Buys in bulk and 'breaks bulk' for small retailers. - Provides storage (warehousing). - Offers credit to retailers. - Provides market information to manufacturers. However, many manufacturers are now 'eliminating the middleman' to reduce prices for consumers. Factors choosing a channel: nature of the product (perishable goods need short channels), cost, location of customers, and the scale of production. E-commerce (selling online) has further shortened distribution channels globally.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe transitioned to the Heritage-Based Education 2024-2030 Curriculum to align with Vision 2030. This framework replaces the old Competence-Based Curriculum. It focuses on five pillars: (1) Research, (2) Innovation, (3) Industrialisation, (4) Teaching, and (5) Community Service. The goal is to produce learners who are 'Global Citizens with a Zimbabwean heart'. Key changes include the introduction of School-Based Projects (SBPs) and a streamlined subject list. By 2026, the curriculum aims to have fully integrated vocational training pathways alongside academic routes to ensure every student leaves school with a practical skill set.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: From 2024 onwards, the Continuous Assessment Learning Activities (CALA) were replaced by School-Based Projects (SBPs). Key features of SBPs: 1. Only ONE project per subject per year is required, unlike the multiple CALA tasks. 2. Assessment Weighting: SBPs account for 20% of the final mark, while the ZIMSEC summative exam accounts for 80%. 3. Focus: SBPs are designed to be more practical and less burdensome for both teachers and learners, emphasizing problem-solving within the local community. The first ZIMSEC exams using the full SBP 20/80 model will occur in 2025 for Grade 7, Form 4, and Form 6.

subject: Economics
content: Introduced in April 2024, the Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) is the nation's latest currency, backed by a composite basket of foreign currency and precious metals (mainly gold). As of 2025/2026, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) maintains a tight monetary policy to ensure ZiG stability. The currency's value is linked to the market price of gold. For Economics students, this represents a shift from pure fiat currency to a commodity-backed system. Success depends on maintaining adequate reserves and public confidence. The 2026 outlook focuses on full dedollarization and the stabilization of the exchange rate to curb inflation and promote industrial growth.

subject: Geography
topic: Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management in Zimbabwe
content: Zimbabwe faces significant climate challenges, including the severe El Niño-induced drought of 2024. The 2025-2026 Geography syllabus emphasizes Disaster Risk Management (DRM). Key strategies include: 1. Irrigation Expansion: Moving away from rain-fed agriculture. 2. Cloud Seeding: Managed by the Meteorological Services Department. 3. Climate-Smart Agriculture (Pfumvudza/Intwasa): Focusing on moisture conservation. 4. Early Warning Systems: Using satellite data to predict weather patterns. Students must understand the impact of global warming on the frequency of cyclones (like Idai) and the shrinking of the Victoria Falls during extreme dry seasons.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Career Pathways in the New Curriculum
content: The 2024 Heritage-Based curriculum introduces five distinct 'Career Pathways' at Advanced Level: 1. STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics): For future scientists and engineers. 2. Visual and Performing Arts (VPA): Focusing on film, music, and theatre. 3. Humanities: Exploring history, sociology, and heritage. 4. Commercials: Business, accounting, and economics. 5. Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET): Practical trades like building, textile, and metal technology. This system allows students to specialize earlier and aligns their education with the Zimbabwe National Qualifications Framework (ZNQF).
source: Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE) 2024

subject: Computer Science
topic: Software Engineering and AI in Zimbabwe
content: Software Engineering has been elevated within the A-Level Commercials and STEM pathways as of 2025. The syllabus now includes: 1. Agile Methodology: Modern project management. 2. Artificial Intelligence (AI) Ethics: Understanding the impact of AI on Zimbabwean society. 3. Cyber Security: Protecting national infrastructure. 4. Mobile App Development: Using Kotlin and Java. This shift reflects the government's drive towards a digital economy. Students are expected to build functional prototypes for their School-Based Projects (SBPs), solving local problems like digital payments or agricultural monitoring.

subject: Agriculture
content: The 2025/2026 Agriculture syllabus shifts focus from subsistence farming to 'Agribusiness'. 1. Value Addition: Processing raw crops (e.g., making peanut butter from groundnuts) to increase profit. 2. Agrotechnology: Using drones for crop spraying and IoT for soil moisture sensing. 3. Export Markets: Understanding the requirements for selling blueberries and citrus to China and the EU. 4. Farm Records: Treating the farm as a business with balance sheets and cash flow statements. This approach aims to make agriculture an attractive career for youths and to achieve national food security through innovation.

subject: History
topic: The Second Chimurenga and National Independence
content: The Second Chimurenga was a protracted armed struggle (1966-1979) against the Rhodesian minority government. After years of fighting, the Lancaster House Agreement was signed in December 1979 to end the war. This led to democratic elections in early 1980. Zimbabwe finally gained its official and full Independence on April 18, 1980. Although the war ended in 1979, 1980 is the correct year of independence.

subject: Family and Religious Studies
content: Family and Religious Studies (FRS) in the Heritage-Based curriculum emphasizes the role of Indigenous Religion. It explores: 1. Concept of God (Mwari/Nyadenga). 2. Ancestors (Vadzimu/Amadlozi) as intermediaries. 3. Sacred sites (e.g., Matonjeni, Great Zimbabwe). 4. Ethics: 'Unhu/Ubuntu' (humanity/respect). The syllabus compares these traditions with Christianity and Islam, promoting religious tolerance and a deeper understanding of Zimbabwean cultural heritage. It highlights how indigenous values of communalism and respect for the environment are vital for modern nation-building.

subject: History
content: Robert Gabriel Mugabe (21 February 1924 - 6 September 2019) was a Zimbabwean revolutionary and politician who served as Prime Minister of Zimbabwe from 1980 to 1987 and then as President from 1987 to 2017. He was a co-founder of ZANU. He is the founding leader of independent Zimbabwe. Robert Mugabe died on 6 September 2019 in Singapore at the age of 95.

subject: Social Science
content: At the primary level (Grade 1-7), Social Science is now 'Family and Heritage Studies'. It covers: 1. My Family: Roles and responsibilities. 2. My School: History and symbols. 3. National Identity: The Flag, National Anthem, and the Coat of Arms. 4. Heritage Sites: Visiting places like Khami Ruins and Hwange National Park. 5. Patriotic Values: Loyalty, honesty, and hard work. The goal is to instill a sense of pride and belonging in young learners, helping them understand where they come from and their role in the future of Zimbabwe.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe's national symbols represent the country's history and aspirations. 1. The National Flag: Green (agriculture), Yellow (minerals), Red (blood shed for independence), Black (native people), White (peace), Zimbabwe Bird (national emblem), Red Star (internationalism/socialism). 2. The Zimbabwe Bird: Based on soapstone carvings found at Great Zimbabwe, it is the national emblem. 3. The Coat of Arms: Features two Kudus, the Zimbabwe Bird, the Red Star, and the motto 'Unity, Freedom, Work'. 4. The National Anthem: 'Simudzai Mureza WeZimbabwe' (Blessed be the Land of Zimbabwe), which celebrates the beauty of the land and the struggle for freedom.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: The Constitution of Zimbabwe (2013) is the supreme law. It includes a comprehensive Bill of Rights. Key features: 1. Separation of Powers: Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary. 2. Devolution: Shifting power to provinces and local authorities. 3. Recognition of 16 official languages. Recent amendments (up to 2024/2025) have focused on the appointment of judges and the extension of the women's and youth quotas in Parliament. Understanding the constitution is a core component of the Heritage Studies syllabus, ensuring citizens know their rights and responsibilities.

subject: General Studies
content: As of 2026, Zimbabwe is making strides towards 'Upper Middle-Income Status' by 2030. Key focus areas: 1. Infrastructure: Completion of the Mbudzi Interchange and expansion of the Beitbridge-Harare highway. 2. Mining: The growth of the Lithium sector (e.g., Bikita and Sabi Star mines) becoming a major export earner. 3. Energy: Increased power generation from Hwange 7 & 8 and new solar farms. 4. Agriculture: Self-sufficiency in wheat and maize despite climate fluctuations. The 2026 'State of the Nation' reflects a period of consolidation, digital transformation, and continued emphasis on heritage-based innovation.

subject: Indigenous Language and Literature
topic: Shona and Ndebele: Heritage and Oral Traditions
content: The compulsory Indigenous Language and Literature syllabus (Shona/Ndebele) merges linguistic mastery with cultural heritage. It emphasizes: 1. Tsumo neZvirahwe (Proverbs and Riddles): Teaching wisdom and critical thinking. 2. Nhoroondo neTsika (History and Customs): Exploring traditional marriage (Roora/Amalobolo), burial rites, and respect for elders. 3. Literature: Analyzing novels and poetry that reflect the Zimbabwean struggle and identity. Students are assessed on their ability to use 'Unhu/Ubuntu' values in their writing and speech, ensuring the preservation of indigenous knowledge for future generations.

subject: Business Enterprise
content: Business Enterprise Skills (formerly Business Studies) focuses on creating entrepreneurs rather than employees. 1. Identifying Opportunities: Using local resources like granite, sun (solar), and land to start businesses. 2. Financial Literacy: Managing budgets, understanding taxes (ZIMRA), and mobile money (EcoCash) integration. 3. Business Ethics: Applying 'Ubuntu' in trade—fairness, community benefit, and integrity. 4. SBPs: Students must develop a mini-business plan or prototype as part of their 20% School-Based Project mark. This subject is key to achieving Vision 2030's goal of an innovation-led economy.

subject: Physics
content: Physics in the STEM pathway (Forms 3-4) emphasizes practical application. 1. Mechanics: Understanding forces, motion, and energy—vital for the growing engineering sector in Zimbabwe. 2. Electricity: Focus on circuits and the national grid. 3. Renewable Energy: Solar energy technology is a major component, reflecting Zimbabwe's shift towards green energy solutions. 4. Electronics: Basic components and their use in local innovations. Physics students are encouraged to build practical devices like solar chargers or water pumps for their School-Based Projects.

subject: Biology
content: The 2024-2030 Biology syllabus connects biological principles to national needs. 1. Genetics: Understanding heredity and its application in breeding drought-resistant crops. 2. Ecology: Conserving Zimbabwe's biodiversity and managing wildlife in parks like Mana Pools. 3. Health: Focus on infectious diseases (Malaria, HIV/AIDS) and the science of nutrition using local foods (e.g., Baobab, Sorghum). 4. Biotechnology: Introduction to tissue culture and its role in modernizing the agricultural sector. The subject aims to produce future doctors, biotechnologists, and environmental scientists.

subject: Chemistry
content: Chemistry focus shifts towards 'Beneficiation'—adding value to raw minerals before export. 1. Mineral Processing: The chemistry of gold, lithium, and platinum extraction. 2. Organic Chemistry: Focus on polymers and local production of soaps and detergents. 3. Analytical Chemistry: Testing water quality and soil PH for farmers. 4. Green Chemistry: Minimizing environmental impact of mining. Students learn how chemical processes can transform Zimbabwe from a raw material exporter to a manufactured goods producer, aligning with the Industrialisation pillar of Education 5.0.

subject: Music
content: Music in the Visual and Performing Arts pathway explores the soul of the nation. 1. Traditional Instruments: Mastering the Mbira, Hosho, and Ngoma. 2. History: Evolution of music from liberation songs (Chimurenga music) to modern genres like Zimdancehall. 3. Theory: Notation, composition, and digital music production. 4. Music Business: Copyright laws and marketing. Students are required to perform at least one traditional piece and one original composition for their practical assessment, preserving the country's rich musical heritage while embracing modern technology.

subject: Theatre Arts
content: Theatre Arts uses performance to address community issues. 1. Indigenous Theatre: Storytelling (Ngano), dance-drama, and ritual performance. 2. Modern Drama: Scriptwriting, directing, and stage management. 3. Theatre for Development: Using performance to educate the public on health, environment, and social justice. 4. Film Studies: Introduction to cinematography and digital editing. The syllabus encourages students to document local oral histories and turn them into stage plays or short films, contributing to the nation's cultural archive.

subject: Physical Education
content: Physical Education, Sports and Mass Displays (PESMD) is now a full academic subject. 1. Sports Science: Anatomy, physiology, and nutrition for athletes. 2. Practical Skills: Mastery of at least two sports (e.g., Football, Netball, Cricket). 3. Mass Displays: Choreographed movements representing national unity and pride, often seen at Independence Day celebrations. 4. Sports Management: Organizing tournaments and coaching basics. The subject prepares students for careers in professional sports, physiotherapy, and fitness management, emphasizing 'podium performance' for national pride.

subject: Building Technology
content: Part of the TVET pathway, Building Technology provides hands-on construction skills. 1. Bricklaying and Plastering: Mastery of structural work. 2. Plan Reading: Interpreting architectural drawings. 3. Sustainable Building: Using local, eco-friendly materials and designing for climate resilience. 4. Entrepreneurship: How to run a construction company. Students complete a practical building project (e.g., a wall or small structure) as their SBP. This subject directly supports the national infrastructure drive, ensuring a skilled workforce for housing and industrial projects.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Advanced Level Humanities students explore deep themes in Indigenous Literature. 1. Post-Colonial Analysis: How Shona and Ndebele writers respond to the colonial experience. 2. Cultural Resilience: Themes of land, identity, and the struggle between tradition and modernity. 3. Linguistic Aesthetics: The use of deep metaphors and idioms to convey complex social truths. 4. Comparative Studies: Comparing Zimbabwean works with other African literatures. This subject fosters a high level of critical thinking and a profound appreciation for the intellectual depth of Zimbabwean culture.

subject: Wood Technology
content: Wood Technology (formerly Woodwork) focuses on the sustainable use of Zimbabwe's timber resources (e.g., Teak, Mahogany). 1. Joints and Construction: Mastering Mortise and Tenon, Dovetail, and Housing joints. 2. Design and Realization: Creating functional furniture from sketches. 3. Power Tools and Safety: Safe operation of lathes, planers, and saws. 4. Finishing: Lacquering and polishing techniques. Students build a significant piece of furniture for their School-Based Project, preparing them for the manufacturing sector.

subject: Metal Technology
content: Metal Technology prepares students for the engineering and manufacturing industries. 1. Welding and Fabrication: Arc, Gas, and Brazing techniques. 2. Machining: Operating lathes and milling machines. 3. Metallurgy: Properties of ferrous and non-ferrous metals. 4. Technical Drawing: Creating engineering blueprints. The syllabus emphasizes 'Industrialisation' by teaching students how to design and produce spare parts and agricultural implements locally.

subject: Textile Technology
content: Textile Technology (formerly Fashion and Fabrics) focuses on the clothing industry. 1. Garment Construction: Pattern drafting, cutting, and sewing. 2. Textile Science: Understanding natural and synthetic fibers. 3. Design and Aesthetics: Applying principles of art to fashion. 4. Value Addition: Dyeing and printing on local cotton. Students design and stitch a complete outfit for their SBP, with an emphasis on creating Zimbabwean-branded apparel.

subject: Art and Design
content: Art and Design in the VPA pathway fosters creative expression. 1. Fine Art: Drawing, painting, and sculpture using local media (e.g., soapstone, clay). 2. Graphic Design: Logo design and visual branding. 3. Heritage Art: Studying the motifs of Great Zimbabwe and San Rock Art. 4. Exhibition: Presenting work to the public. The syllabus encourages students to use art as a tool for national storytelling and as a viable career in the creative economy.
source: ZIMSEC Art and Design VPA Syllabus 2024

subject: Shona
content: Muchidzidzo cheChiShona, mazita akakamurwa kuita mipanda yakasiyana-siyana (Noun Classes). Kuparadzaniswa uku kunobva pamavambirwo emazita (prefixes). 1. Mupanda 1 ne2 (mu-/va-): Unoshandiswa kumazita evanhu, semuenzaniso: munhu/vanhu, mudzidzisi/vadzidzisi. 2. Mupanda 7 ne8 (chi-/zvi-): Unoshandiswa kuzvinhu kana mitauro, semuenzaniso: chigaro/zvigaro, ChiShona. 3. Mupanda 9 ne10 (i-/dzi-): Unoshandiswa kumhuka nezvimwe zvinhu, semuenzaniso: imbwa/dzimbwa, nzou. 4. Mupanda 11 (ru-): Unoshandiswa kuzvinhu zvakatetepa kana zvakareba, semuenzaniso: ruoko, rutsoka. Kuziva mipanda kunobatsira pakururamisa mutauro nekuwiriranisa zviito (concordial agreement).

subject: Shona
content: Tsumo dzinoshandiswa kupa mazano, kuraira, kana kutsiura munhu zvine huchenjeri. 1. 'Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda': Tsumo iyi inoreva kuti kubatana ndiko kune simba. Munhu haakwanisi kuita basa guru ari oga. 2. 'Kure kwegava ndokusina mutsubvu': Inoreva kuti kana munhu achida chinhu zvakaoma, anoita zvese zvaanokwanisa kuti achiwane, pasinei nekure kwacho. 3. 'Rinonyenga rinohwarara, rine kachiri kanozvitwura': Inoreva kuti munhu anokumbira ruyamuro anozvininipisa, asi kana achinge awana zvaanoda anogona kuzvikudza. 4. 'Kugara nhaka huona dzevamwe': Inodzidzisa kuti tinofanira kutevedzera zvinhu zvakanaka zvatinoona zvichiitwa nevamwe.

subject: Shona
content: Madimikira mazwi anoshandiswa kureva chimwe chinhu nenzira isiri iyo chaiyo yamazwi acho. 1. 'Kubereka tsoka': Kutiza zvakanyanya kana kuvamba rwendo nekukurumidza. 2. 'Kurova pasi': Kufa kana kureva kuti munhu haachipo. 3. 'Kudya marasha': Kutsamwa zvakanyanya kana kuva nehasha. 4. 'Kupisa tsoka': Kufamba rwendo rurefu. 5. 'Kuzvisikiramoto muziso': Kuzvitsvakira dambudziko pachako. Madimikira anobatsira kuti mutauro uve unotapira uye unonakidza kuteerera kana kuverenga.

subject: Shona
content: Nyaudzosingwi mazwi anotsanangura chiitiko kana ruzha nenzira pfupi uye ine simba. 1. 'Go': Ruzha rwekurova chinhu chakaoma. 2. 'Pwa': Ruzha rwekupwanyiwa kwechinhu. 3. 'N'ai': Kupenya kwechiedza semheni kana girazi. 4. 'Nyu': Kunyura mumvura. 5. 'Mupupu': Kusvika kwechinhu nekukurumidza. 6. 'N'u': Kunhuwa kwechinhu chakaora. Nyaudzosingwi dzinobatsira kutsanangura zviitiko kuti zvive nemufananidzo mupfungwa dzemuteereri.

subject: Shona
content: Unhu kana kuti Ubuntu hwaro hwekuti munhu ave nemagariro akanaka munharaunda. 1. Kudanana nekuwadzana nevamwe: Munhu haagoni kurarama oga (Munhu munhu nevanhu). 2. Kuremekedza vakuru: Kukudza vabereki nevanhu vose vakura kupfuura iwe. 3. Kutambira vaeni: Kuva nemwoyo muchene kune vashanyi. 4. Kuzvininipisa: Kusazvikudza pasinei nekubudirira kwako. 5. Kubatsira vanoshaya: Kuva nemwoyo wekupa kune avo vasina. Izvi ndizvo zvinoita kuti nhoroondo netsika dzeZimbabwe dzive dzakasimba uye dzichiremekedzwa pasi rose.

subject: Shona
content: Uvaranomwe hweChiShona hwakakamurwa kuita zvikamu zvitatu zvikuru: 1. Ngano: Idzi nyaya dzekare dzaidzidziswa nevanasekuru kana vanambuya manheru (Traditional Folktales). Dzaive nechinangwa chekudzidzisa tsika neunhu. 2. Nhetembo: Kushandiswa kwemazwi nenzira ine mufananidzo (imagery) nekurira kwakanaka kutsanangura manzwiro kana nhoroondo. 3. Mitambo (Drama): Nyaya dzinotambwa nevanhu pachikuva dzichiratidza matambudziko kana mufaro wevanhu. Mudzidzi anofanira kuongorora vanyori (authors), dingindira (themes), nekurukuro (plot) yeaya mabhuku.

subject: Shona
content: Kudzidza Shona kunotanga nekuziva kukwazisana. 1. Mangwanani: Good morning. (Mhinduro: Mamuka sei? - Tamuka kana mamukawo). 2. Masikati: Good afternoon. (Mhinduro: Maswera sei? - Taswera kana maswerawo). 3. Manheru: Good evening. 4. Ndatenda: Thank you. 5. Ndapota: Please. 6. Chienda zvakanaka: Go well. 7. Sara zvakanaka: Stay well. 8. Maita basa: Well done / Thank you for the work. Kuziva mazwi aya kunovhura mikova yekuwadzana nevanhu vanotaura ChiShona muZimbabwe.

subject: Mathematics
content: For ZIMSEC 4004/4075 Paper 2: 1. Quadratic Formula: x = [-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a. 2. Trigonometry: SOH CAH TOA (Sin = Opp/Hyp, Cos = Adj/Hyp, Tan = Opp/Adj). Sine Rule: a/SinA = b/SinB. Cosine Rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bcCosA. 3. Mensuration: Area of Circle = pi*r^2. Volume of Cylinder = pi*r^2*h. Volume of Cone = (1/3)*pi*r^2*h. Volume of Sphere = (4/3)*pi*r^3. 4. Indices: a^m * a^n = a^(m+n). a^m / a^n = a^(m-n). (a^m)^n = a^(mn). 5. Logarithms: log(ab) = log a + log b. log(a/b) = log a - log b. log(a^n) = n log a. Understanding these is essential for solving Paper 2 section B problems correctly.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Pure Math: Core Calculus and Vectors
content: Advanced Level Pure Mathematics (6042) high-weight areas: 1. Differentiation: Product Rule, Quotient Rule, and Chain Rule. Applications in finding stationary points and rates of change. 2. Integration: Integration by Parts, Substitution, and Partial Fractions. Definite integrals for area under curves and volumes of revolution. 3. Vectors in 3D: Dot Product (scalar product) to find angles between vectors. Line and Plane equations. 4. Series: Summation of arithmetic and geometric progressions. Binomial expansion for any rational index. 5. Complex Numbers: Operations in Cartesian form (a + bi) and Polar form (r cis theta). De Moivre's Theorem for powers and roots of complex numbers.

subject: Ndebele
content: IsiNdebele silendlela eqondileyo yokuhlela amabizo ngeziqalo zawo (Noun Classes/Izizigaba). 1. Isigaba 1 le-2 (umu-/aba-): Sibizwa kakhulu ngezinto eziphilayo (abantu), njengokuthi: umuntu/abantu, umfundisi/abafundisi. 2. Isigaba 7 le-8 (isi-/izi-): Sisetshenziswa ezintweni zemizimba, izinto eziphathekayo, lemitshina, njengokuthi: isihlalo/izihlalo, isandla/izandla. 3. Isigaba 9 le-10 (i-/izi-): Sibizwa kakhulu ngezifuyo lamazwi athathwe kwezinye izindimi, njengokuthi: inja/izinja, inkomo/izinkomo. 4. Isigaba 11 (u-): Sisetshenziswa ezintweni ezinde kakhulu, njengokuthi: upondo, unwele. Ukwazi izizigaba kuqakathekile ekwakheni imithetho yolimi eqondileyo.

subject: Ndebele
content: Izaga ziveza ukuhlakanipha lesiko leSindebele. 1. 'Izandla ziyagezana': Kutsho ukuthi abantu kumele basizane (Helping each other). 2. 'Inja iyawaqeda amabele': Kutsho ukuthi umuntu owehlulekayo ukuziphatha angona izinto ezinhle (Lack of self-control ruins prospects). 3. 'Umntwana ongakhaliyo ufela embelekweni': Kutsho ukuthi kumele ukhulume uma udinga usizo (Ask for help if you need it). 4. 'Kuzwakala okungatshoyo': Kutsho ukuthi kukhona okubi okwenzakalayo (Something unexpected/bad is happening). Zitsho: 'Ukubamba ithambo' (To work hard), 'Ukubeka amadodana' (To have a discussion), 'Ukubeka ihlombe' (To help/support).

subject: Chemistry
topic: Industrial Processes: Haber, Contact and Blast Furnace
content: High-frequency exam topics in ZIMSEC Chemistry: 1. Haber Process: Production of Ammonia (NH3) from Nitrogen and Hydrogen. Conditions: 450C, 200 atm pressure, Iron catalyst. Uses: Fertilizers and cleaning agents. 2. Contact Process: Production of Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4). Key steps: Sulfur -> SO2 -> SO3 -> Oleum -> H2SO4. Catalyst: Vanadium (V) Oxide. 3. Blast Furnace: Extraction of Iron from Hematite (Fe2O3). Raw materials: Iron ore, Limestone (to remove sand as slag), and Coke (reducing agent). 4. Fractional Distillation of Crude Oil: Separation based on boiling points into fractions like Petrol, Diesel, and Bitumen. 5. Electrolysis: Production of Chlorine and Aluminum. Understanding chemical equations for these is critical for Paper 2.

subject: Literature in English
topic: Set Books Analysis: Shadows and Othello
content: For the 2025/2026 cycle: 1. 'Shadows on the Horizon' (Stephen Mpofu): Explores themes of the liberation struggle, post-colonial disappointment, and the search for identity in modern Zimbabwe. 2. 'I Will Wait' (Bertha Musora): Focuses on gender roles, perseverance, and the impact of traditional vs modern values on families. 3. 'Othello' (Shakespeare): Themes of Jealousy (the 'green-eyed monster'), Manipulation (Iago's villainy), Racism, and Betrayal. Students should focus on character development and 'Dramatic Irony'. 4. 'The Valley of Tantalika': Nature vs Civilization and the environmental cost of development (Kariba Dam construction).

subject: Physics
topic: A-Level Physics: Mechanics and Quantum Basics
content: Advanced Level Physics (6032) focus: 1. Newtonian Mechanics: Newton's Laws (F=ma, Action-Reaction), Circular Motion, and Gravitational Fields. Centripetal force F = mv^2/r. 2. Oscillations: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM). Displacement x = A sin(wt). 3. Modern/Quantum Physics: The Photoelectric Effect (E = hf - Phi). Wave-particle duality and the De Broglie wavelength. 4. Nuclear Physics: Radioactive decay laws, Binding Energy per nucleon, and Fission/Fusion processes. 5. Electricity: Kirchhoff's Laws (Sum of currents = 0, Sum of EMF = Sum of IR), Capacitance (C = Q/V), and Magnetic induction.

subject: Geography
content: New high-frequency areas for Geography (6037): 1. GIS (Geographic Information Systems): Data collection (Remote sensing, GPS), data storage (Vector vs Raster models), and Data Analysis (Buffering, Overlays). GIS is now compulsory for Paper 3. 2. Urbanization in Zimbabwe: Causes (Rural-to-Urban migration), consequences (Growth of informal settlements like Epworth/Hopley, pressure on water/electricity), and solutions (Devolution, Urban renewal). 3. Hydrology: The hydrograph (Lag time, peak discharge) and drainage basin features. 4. Geomorphology: Plate tectonics (Divergent/Convergent boundaries) and Slope development models (Penck vs King).
